title: Cal AI's 19-Year-Old Founder Raises $10M for New AI Startup Persona
excerpt: Zach Yadegari, whose calorie-tracking app was acquired by MyFitnessPal, raised $10 million led by Vine Ventures for Persona — an AI assistant starting in iMessage and moving to a $179 wristband.
body:
• Zach Yadegari, the 19-year-old co-founder of Cal AI, has raised $10 million for his new startup Persona, led by Vine Ventures with Z Fellows founder Cory Levy and Collective Global participating.
  • Persona is a personal AI assistant that starts as a free iMessage beta and is designed to move onto a $179 screenless wristband shipping in December 2026.
  • The 27-gram aluminum band has two microphones, a speaker and an LED ring instead of a display; it activates by button or wrist gesture, is claimed to understand 120 languages, and offers about three days of battery.
  • Why it matters: Yadegari sold his first business at 16, built Cal AI to more than 15 million downloads and over $30 million in annual revenue before its MyFitnessPal acquisition — investors are betting the teenager's viral-growth playbook works a second time.

Zach Yadegari is 19, and he has already built, scaled and sold one AI company. Now he has $10 million to try it again. The Cal AI co-founder has raised a new round for Persona, his personal-AI-assistant startup, led by Vine Ventures with participation from Z Fellows founder Cory Levy and Collective Global, TechCrunch reported Thursday.

The $10 million round

Terms and valuation were not disclosed. Persona's early traction is company-reported but notable: a few thousand beta users, and band preorders that have already generated five figures in revenue. The round is separate from earlier September reports of a $5 million raise tied to the band's launch — Thursday's announcement is a new, larger bet.

What Persona is

Persona starts as a free beta inside iMessage and is designed to migrate onto a $179 wearable wristband shipping in December 2026. The ambition is to handle routine tasks across services — booking appointments and rides, managing messages and email, taking notes, answering questions, booking travel, ordering food — without opening each app. Yadegari's larger thesis is that everyday utility apps will be consolidated into a single assistant.

The hardware is deliberately minimal: a screenless, 27-gram aluminum wristband with two microphones, a speaker and an LED ring instead of a display. It activates with a button press or a wrist gesture — deliberate activation, not an always-open microphone — and responds to voice commands or on-wrist taps. The company claims it understands 120 languages, lasts about three days on a charge, charges over USB-C, is waterproof, and lets users mute the dual microphones.

"Sits on hold, argues the fee, and calls back until it's sorted."

— Persona, on the kind of tasks its AI assistant is designed to handle

The pitch examples from the launch are deliberately mundane: an assistant that sits on hold with customer service, argues the fee and calls back until it is sorted; one that sends invoices, chases late payments and follows up with clients. Yadegari's framing of the AI-hardware landscape is blunt — he said other developers "couldn't figure out the interface" — and his answer is to remove the screen entirely.

The Cal AI backstory

Yadegari co-founded Cal AI as a teenager — at 17, with fellow high school students — as a photo-based AI calorie-tracking app that estimated calories from food photos. It exploded: more than 15 million downloads and over $30 million in annual revenue in under two years. MyFitnessPal acquired the company in a deal that closed in December 2025 and was announced in March 2026; the price was not disclosed.

Yadegari joined MyFitnessPal with his co-founders after the acquisition, then left in June 2026 to start Persona. It was not his first exit: in ninth grade he built a gaming business and sold it for $100,000 at age 16. He is also slated for a fireside chat on viral growth at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

Why investors are betting again

AI hardware has a graveyard — ambitious devices that could not find a daily use case. Yadegari's counterargument is distribution: Cal AI grew through the same teenage viral playbook that took it from a school project to a nine-figure acquisition, and Persona's iMessage-first strategy is built to spread the same way before the band ever ships. Whether a screenless wristband earns a place on people's arms is the December question. For now, $10 million says the people who missed Cal AI are not missing Persona.
